title: Cymraeg: The Language They Could Not Silence
deck: From the humiliation of children punished for speaking Welsh to generations fighting for the right to learn, work, and live through their mother tongue, the story of Cymraeg is one of institutional discrimination, cultural endurance, and a future still being shaped.

sections.heading: When a Child's Own Language Became a Reason for Punishment
sections.body:
Imagine arriving at school and discovering that the language you speak at home is considered something you should be ashamed of.

The words you learned from your parents, the language of your grandparents, the familiar expressions that give shape to your earliest memories—suddenly, those same words can bring punishment.

For some children in nineteenth-century Wales, this was reality.

Welsh, known to its speakers as *Cymraeg*, was not a language without history, literature, or cultural significance. It possessed one of Europe's oldest surviving vernacular literary traditions and had been spoken across generations of communities.

It was a language of poetry, religious worship, publishing, conversation, and everyday life.

Yet as English became increasingly dominant in government, education, commerce, and public advancement, Welsh-speaking communities faced mounting pressure to adapt to institutions that often gave their own language little respect.

In some classrooms, children were discouraged from speaking Welsh. In others, they could be humiliated or physically punished for using it.

And in 1847, an official education inquiry produced reports containing disparaging judgments about Welsh language, religion, and society.

The injustice was not simply that one language was becoming more powerful than another.

It was that a language spoken by generations of people could be treated as a mark of inferiority by institutions responsible for their education and advancement.

But Welsh did not disappear.

Its speakers continued to use it in homes, communities, literature, worship, and cultural life. Later generations organized campaigns to secure greater recognition and rights.

Today, Welsh is an official language in Wales, children can receive education through it, and communities continue working to secure its place in everyday life.

Its survival is a remarkable achievement.

But the story is neither an uncomplicated victory nor a struggle that has ended.

---

sections.heading: 01 — When Schools Taught Children That Welsh Was Inferior
sections.body:
### A language of home and community confronted the authority of English.

To understand the pressures Welsh speakers experienced in nineteenth-century education, it is necessary to understand the growing institutional power of English.

English had become central to government administration, legal authority, and many forms of economic and educational advancement.

Welsh remained widely spoken, particularly in areas where it was the language of ordinary community life. But its strong position among speakers did not guarantee equal treatment in public institutions.

In schools, the imbalance was especially damaging.

Children could arrive speaking Welsh fluently but with limited knowledge of English. Rather than consistently using their existing language as a foundation for education, some schools treated Welsh as an obstacle that had to be overcome.

For certain children, that attitude was enforced through punishment.

### The Welsh Not: Punishment for Speaking Your Mother Tongue

Among the most troubling symbols of Welsh-language discrimination was the **Welsh Not**.

The Welsh Not was a token, often made of wood, used in some nineteenth-century schools to identify children caught speaking Welsh.

Museum Wales documents its use at Maestir School.

Children found speaking Welsh could be made to wear the token. Pupils were encouraged to report one another, passing the object to another child caught using the language.

At the end of the school day, the child left holding it was caned.

Consider what such a system demanded of children.

They had to monitor the language in which they naturally spoke. They could be encouraged to report friends and classmates. They risked punishment not for harming someone, cheating, or refusing to learn, but for speaking Welsh.

A child's mother tongue had become something to conceal.

The system also placed pressure on relationships between children. A classmate's use of Welsh could become an opportunity to transfer punishment elsewhere.

This was more than a harsh educational practice.

It was a method of enforcing a linguistic hierarchy.

English was treated as the language of schooling and advancement. Welsh, despite its long history and continued use in the surrounding community, could be treated as a problem.

There is an essential historical distinction: the Welsh Not was not imposed through one nationwide law requiring identical punishments in every Welsh school.

Its use differed between schools and periods. Not every Welsh-speaking child experienced it.

But documented cases do not become less serious because the practice was not universal.

**Some children were physically punished for speaking the language they had learned at home. That is the historical injustice at the heart of the Welsh Not.**

### 1847 — The Treachery of the Blue Books

In 1847, a government inquiry into education in Wales produced three reports that became known as the *Blue Books*.

The inquiry was conducted by three commissioners who did not speak Welsh.

Their reports addressed problems in Welsh education, but they also contained deeply prejudiced judgments about the Welsh language and aspects of Welsh society, including religion and morality.

The reports became notorious not simply because they identified educational shortcomings, but because of the attitudes through which Welsh-speaking communities were assessed.

Educational inequality was a legitimate subject of investigation.

But the inquiry's disparaging treatment of Welsh language and culture contributed to the idea that Welsh itself was an impediment to progress.

The reaction was fierce.

The reports became known as **Brad y Llyfrau Gleision**—*the Treachery of the Blue Books*.

The name reflected the sense of betrayal provoked by an official investigation whose conclusions could be understood as an attack on the character and culture of the people it was supposed to serve.

Its influence extended beyond the immediate controversy.

The Blue Books strengthened the association between English and educational advancement, while contributing to the stigma surrounding Welsh.

This mattered enormously for families.

Parents wanted their children to succeed. They wanted access to education, employment, and opportunities that might make life easier than it had been for previous generations.

But what happens when the institutions controlling those opportunities repeatedly favor another language?

Families can begin to face a painful choice.

They may continue speaking the language they love while encouraging their children to prioritize the language associated with power.

They may fear that passing on their own language will expose children to disadvantage.

And over time, such pressures can influence which language is passed from one generation to the next.

**A community does not need to stop loving its language for that language to become vulnerable. Sometimes the pressure is so great that parents begin to fear what speaking it might cost their children.**

---

sections.heading: 02 — A Language That Refused to Disappear
sections.body:
### Welsh survived because it remained part of people's lives.

The history of Welsh should never be reduced to a story of repression followed by rescue.

Welsh was never simply absent, waiting for modern institutions to restore it.

Throughout periods of educational and political inequality, it remained a language of homes, communities, religious life, literature, journalism, and cultural expression.

The Welsh literary tradition continued to develop. Writers, poets, publishers, and religious communities helped maintain Welsh as a language capable of expressing intellectual, spiritual, and everyday experience.

Cultural traditions such as the Eisteddfod provided important opportunities for literary and artistic expression through Welsh.

The language remained alive because people continued using it.

Yet endurance did not mean that institutional pressure was harmless.

### The Difficult Choices Families Faced

During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, economic change, migration, urbanization, and English-dominant institutions altered the linguistic circumstances of communities across Wales.

English increasingly offered access to forms of education and employment that families understandably wanted for their children.

For some, raising children with greater use of English seemed a practical necessity.

That decision should not automatically be interpreted as a rejection of Welsh identity.

It was often made in a society where the rewards associated with English were greater and the institutional support for Welsh was weaker.

Language shift under such circumstances is not simply a story of people freely choosing one language over another.

It is also a story about unequal power.

The consequences could accumulate across generations.

A child educated mainly through English might later use English more frequently at work. Their own children might grow up with fewer opportunities to acquire Welsh naturally.

Eventually, a language that had been central to family life could become something associated more strongly with grandparents, cultural events, or formal lessons.

The change could happen gradually enough to seem ordinary.

Its effects were anything but trivial.

For a language to remain strong, it must continue to be spoken between generations—not only remembered with affection.

### The Growth of Organized Language Activism

The twentieth century brought increasing efforts to challenge the marginalization of Welsh in public life.

One important turning point came in 1962.

That year, Welsh writer and academic Saunders Lewis delivered a radio lecture titled *Tynged yr Iaith*—*The Fate of the Language*.

His address warned about the future of Welsh and helped energize a generation of language activists.

Also in 1962, *Cymdeithas yr Iaith Gymraeg*—the Welsh Language Society—was established.

The organization became a major force in campaigns for Welsh-language rights.

Through protests, direct action, and civil disobedience, activists challenged arrangements that restricted opportunities to use Welsh in public administration, broadcasting, education, and other areas of everyday life.

They pressed institutions to recognize a principle that should have required little explanation:

People living in Wales should have meaningful opportunities to use Welsh in their own country.

The campaigns were not merely about ensuring that Welsh appeared in historical records or ceremonial settings.

They were about whether people could use the language to conduct ordinary business, access services, receive education, and participate in modern society.

### Legal Recognition Arrives

Gradually, legislation began to change the official position of Welsh.

The **Welsh Language Act 1967** expanded opportunities to use Welsh in legal proceedings in Wales and provided for certain official uses of the language.

The **Welsh Language Act 1993** introduced a stronger framework for Welsh in public administration, including the principle that Welsh and English should be treated on a basis of equality in the conduct of public business and the administration of justice in Wales, so far as appropriate and reasonably practicable.

Then, in 2011, the **Welsh Language (Wales) Measure** established Welsh as an official language in Wales and created a statutory framework for Welsh-language standards and rights.

These were substantial changes.

A language that had been stigmatized in nineteenth-century education had gained significant legal recognition.

But no law could undo generations of humiliation, reverse every pattern of language shift, or guarantee that Welsh would become the natural language of every home and workplace.

Legislation could create rights and responsibilities.

The continued life of Welsh would still depend on people having opportunities to use it.

---

sections.heading: 03 — A Language Recognized, but Not Yet Secure
sections.body:
### The question is no longer only whether Welsh is permitted. It is whether Welsh can thrive.

Modern Wales offers opportunities for Welsh that earlier generations worked hard to secure.

Welsh-medium education enables children to learn through the language rather than encountering it solely as a subject.

Welsh-language broadcasting, literature, music, publishing, and digital resources contribute to a contemporary cultural life.

Public institutions operate under legal frameworks intended to support the use of Welsh.

These developments are significant achievements.

They reflect generations of organizing, education, cultural work, legislation, and community commitment.

But a language can have official recognition and still face serious pressures in daily life.

A bilingual sign does not guarantee that Welsh is spoken in the business behind it.

A school can teach Welsh without ensuring that children will continue using it with friends.

Someone may report being able to speak Welsh but have limited opportunities to use it naturally in their community or workplace.

The distinction between knowing a language and regularly using it is essential.

### What the 2021 Census Revealed

The 2021 Census recorded **538,300 people aged three and over in Wales who reported being able to speak Welsh**.

That represented **17.8%** of the population in that age group.

<text>This was lower than the 2011 Census figure of approximately 562,000 speakers, or 19.0%.</text>

<text>The figures refer to reported speaking ability among residents of Wales aged three and over. They do not measure how often each person uses Welsh, their individual level of fluency, or the worldwide Welsh-speaking population.</text>

The decline deserves attention.

It demonstrates why the existence of legal protections, Welsh-medium education, and greater public visibility should not be treated as proof that all threats to the language have been overcome.

Welsh Government has established an ambition of reaching one million Welsh speakers by 2050 through its *Cymraeg 2050* strategy.

It is an ambitious goal.

But ambitions cannot be mistaken for achievements.

Progress requires sustained attention to education, family transmission, community language use, employment, and the social conditions that allow speakers to live through Welsh.

### The Future Depends on Everyday Opportunities

For a language to flourish, it must have a place beyond formal recognition.

Children need opportunities to speak it naturally, not merely answer questions about it in class.

Families need access to supportive educational and community networks.

Young adults need places where using Welsh is practical, welcome, and socially meaningful.

Existing Welsh-speaking communities need conditions that support their continued use of the language.

This last point is particularly important.

Language revitalization cannot be measured only by how many people begin learning Welsh.

It must also consider the communities in which Welsh has remained part of ordinary life.

When those communities experience economic pressure, migration, or declining opportunities to use Welsh, the effects can extend into intergenerational transmission.

A language does not survive only because people know its words.

It survives through the relationships in which those words are spoken.

**The future of Welsh depends not simply on creating more people who can speak it, but on ensuring that people have meaningful reasons and opportunities to keep speaking it.**

---

sections.heading: 04 — Welsh Belongs in the Digital World
sections.body:
### A living language needs room in the places where people communicate today.

Welsh has a rich written history, extending across centuries of manuscripts, poetry, religious texts, journalism, and literature.

Today, much of the written communication that shapes ordinary life happens digitally.

People write messages, complete schoolwork, publish articles, communicate with colleagues, and create new forms of cultural expression through keyboards and screens.

Welsh belongs in those spaces.

Making room for a language in the digital world means more than displaying its name on a list of supported languages.

It means respecting its writing system, ensuring that people can enter its characters accurately, and recognizing that written Welsh has conventions of its own.

### Learning to Type Welsh Accurately

Welsh uses accented vowels, including circumflex forms such as:

**â ê î ô û ŵ ŷ**

The circumflex, often called *to bach*, can distinguish vowel length or meaning in particular words.

Welsh also uses digraphs—pairs of written characters treated as letters within the Welsh alphabet—including:

**ch, dd, ff, ng, ll, ph, rh, th**

These are not unusual combinations to be replaced with more familiar English spellings.

They belong to a distinct linguistic system with its own history and structure.

For typing practice, begin by reproducing written material accurately.

Preserve the accents in the source passage. Pay attention to spelling conventions. Do not remove unfamiliar characters simply to achieve a faster score.

Where possible, connect written practice with listening, pronunciation guidance, and explanations from reliable language-learning materials.

Reading and typing words can support familiarity with the writing system.

They are not substitutes for learning what the words mean or how the language is spoken.

### Why WPMTest Includes Welsh

WPMTest's Living Languages Series explores the histories of languages shaped by unequal institutions, cultural pressure, resilience, and community-led efforts to strengthen their futures.

Welsh belongs in the series because its history demonstrates both the harm that linguistic discrimination can cause and the extraordinary efforts people have made to challenge it.

A typing website cannot undo the humiliation of a child punished for speaking Welsh.

It cannot reverse generations of interrupted transmission or replace the work of Welsh-speaking communities.

But it can introduce readers to the written language, provide carefully sourced historical context, and encourage respectful curiosity about the people working to sustain it.

The WPMTest Welsh pathway currently begins with character and language-name copying exercises, alongside the option to practise with text whose spelling and use rights the reader has independently verified.

It does not yet claim to provide a speaker-reviewed collection of Welsh sentences.

The aim is to support careful introductory engagement—not to suggest that typing exercises alone constitute language learning.

**Words per minute measures typing performance. It cannot measure the cultural significance of a language, the depth of its history, or the knowledge of the people who speak it.**

---

sections.heading: Turning Points in the History of Welsh
sections.body:
**1847 — The Treachery of the Blue Books**

A government education inquiry publishes reports containing prejudiced judgments about Welsh language, religion, and society. The reports provoke widespread anger and become enduring symbols of linguistic and cultural discrimination.

**Nineteenth Century — The Welsh Not**

The Welsh Not is used in some schools to punish children for speaking Welsh. Museum Wales documents the practice at Maestir School, where the child left holding the token at the end of the school day could be caned.

**1962 — A New Era of Language Activism**

Saunders Lewis delivers *Tynged yr Iaith*, warning about the future of Welsh. The Welsh Language Society is founded and becomes an influential force in campaigns for Welsh-language rights.

**1967 — The Welsh Language Act**

Legislation expands opportunities to use Welsh in legal proceedings and certain official settings.

**1993 — A Stronger Public-Language Framework**

The Welsh Language Act establishes a more extensive framework for Welsh in public administration.

**2011 — Official Status for Welsh**

The Welsh Language (Wales) Measure gives Welsh official status in Wales and establishes a framework for Welsh-language standards.

**2021 — The Census Reveals Continuing Challenges**

The Census records 538,300 Welsh speakers aged three and over in Wales, representing 17.8% of the population in that age group.

**2050 — An Ambition for the Future**

The Welsh Government's *Cymraeg 2050* strategy aims to reach one million Welsh speakers by 2050. This is a policy ambition, not an accomplished result.

*These are selected milestones rather than a complete history. The experiences of Welsh speakers differed across communities, generations, and institutions.*

---

sections.heading: The Language They Tried to Silence Is Still Being Spoken
sections.body:
There is a striking contrast at the heart of this history.

In some nineteenth-century classrooms, a child could be punished for speaking Welsh.

Today, children can receive their education through Welsh.

The language that was once treated as an obstacle to learning is now a language through which learning takes place.

That transformation deserves recognition.

But it did not happen because injustice naturally disappears with the passage of time.

It happened through the persistence of speakers, the commitment of families, the work of teachers and writers, and the determination of campaigners who challenged the institutions around them.

The Welsh Not and the Blue Books belong to a history that should not be minimized or forgotten.

Their legacy reminds us how damaging it can be when a society teaches children that the language of their families is less worthy of respect.

Yet the continued life of Welsh tells another part of the story.

Despite discrimination and changing social circumstances, Welsh remained a language of people, communities, literature, and cultural expression.

Later generations worked to expand its place in schools, government, broadcasting, and public life.

Today, that work continues.

There are still challenges in maintaining Welsh-speaking communities, strengthening intergenerational use, and ensuring that legal recognition becomes meaningful opportunity.

The 2021 Census figures remind us that progress cannot be assumed.

But there are also reasons for hope.

Children are learning through Welsh. Families are passing it to new generations. Writers, musicians, educators, broadcasters, and community organizations continue developing its place in contemporary life.

What matters most is not simply that Welsh survived the institutions that once diminished it.

It is that Welsh speakers continue to shape what their language can become.

**A language that some children were once punished for speaking is now the language in which other children can learn, question, imagine, and dream.**

The past cannot be undone.

But it does not have to determine every possibility of the future.

**Cymraeg is not merely a language that endured. It is a living language whose story is still being written.**

---

sections.heading: Sources, Photography, and Editorial Care
sections.body:
This article draws on the following historical, legislative, and institutional materials:

1. [National Library of Wales — The Blue Books of 1847](https://www.library.wales/discover-learn/digital-exhibitions/printed-material/the-blue-books-of-1847) — The 1847 education inquiry and the controversy surrounding its conclusions.

2. [Museum Wales — Maestir School and the Welsh Not](https://museum.wales/collections/historic-buildings/21/Maestir-School/) — Museum documentation concerning the punishment of children for speaking Welsh.

3. [Welsh Government — Welsh Language in Wales, Census 2021](https://www.gov.wales/welsh-language-wales-census-2021-html) — Official figures concerning Welsh-speaking ability and change between censuses.

4. [Welsh Language Act 1967](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1967/66/contents) — Legislation relating to Welsh in legal proceedings and official settings.

5. [Welsh Language Act 1993](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1993/38/enacted/data.html) — Legislation establishing a stronger public-language framework.

6. [Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2011/1/contents) — Legislation concerning the official status of Welsh and Welsh-language standards.

**Additional recommended sources before publication:** The history of Cymdeithas yr Iaith Gymraeg, Saunders Lewis's 1962 lecture *Tynged yr Iaith*, and the Welsh Government's *Cymraeg 2050* strategy.

**Photography**

Tenby Harbour, Pembrokeshire, Wales.

Photograph: [Michel Collignon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tenby_Panorama_view_from_The_Croft_and_Norton_corner.jpg) · [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en).

Location photographs illustrate places associated with the language. They do not represent the experiences or views of every Welsh speaker or community.

**Our Editorial Approach**

The Welsh Not is historically documented, but its use was not universal across Welsh schools.

This article distinguishes the specific practices documented by Museum Wales from broader patterns of educational inequality and language discrimination.

It also recognizes that Welsh has remained a living language throughout the periods discussed, and that Welsh-speaking communities have never shared one identical historical experience.

Historical accounts of injustice should neither minimize the experiences of those affected nor go beyond the available evidence.

This source-based article is not a claim of fluent-speaker or specialist endorsement. New sentence passages require appropriate Welsh-language review before being described as speaker-reviewed.

[Send a Correction or Offer Language Review →](https://wpmtest.app/contact/)
